### Question 4: alternative and simpler panels

For a consistent comparison with Q3 and the class analysis, we used the supplied cleaned dataset, ASD/TD random-forest labels, seed 101422, the same 80/20 split and a fixed 0.5 classification threshold. The class benchmark retains the original full-data t-test/random-forest top-10 intersection. Q4 selected proteins on training subjects and compared the same 24 configurations using three repeats of stratified five-fold training cross-validation. We investigated lasso as the primary alternative and a one- to three-protein panel as a secondary option.

Training cross-validation selects lasso_all_0.2 as the alternative (mean accuracy 74.0%) and fuzzy1 as the smaller approach (mean accuracy 67.5%). Fitting those rules to all training subjects produces 38 and 1 proteins respectively.

| Approach | Proteins | Sensitivity | Specificity | Accuracy | AUROC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| In-class baseline (rerun) | 5 | 81.2% | 73.3% | 77.4% | 0.883 |
| Q4 alternative: lasso_all_0.2 | 38 | 50.0% | 93.3% | 71.0% | 0.925 |
| Q4 simpler: fuzzy1 | 1 | 50.0% | 93.3% | 71.0% | 0.792 |

The alternative has lower observed accuracy than the rerun class baseline. The smaller panel does not meet the descriptive two-percentage-point comparability criterion against the rerun class baseline.

The simpler panel contained DERM. The class panel contained DERM, RELT, MRC2, IgD, Cadherin-5. The alternative's full protein list and coefficients can be regenerated by the accompanying Q4 script.

The alternative's sensitivity is 50.0% versus 81.2% for the class baseline. Overall accuracy, ASD detection and AUROC therefore need separate interpretation; a higher AUROC is not automatically higher accuracy at the fixed 0.5 threshold.

The team's q3_base.R comments record accuracy 83.9% and AUROC 0.908. The class baseline reproduced in this run gives accuracy 77.4% and AUROC 0.883. The historical numbers are not inserted into the current-run table as if they came from this run. The discrepancy cannot be attributed to the metric syntax alone: direct counting and yardstick agree on the current predictions. To resolve differences across computers, compare selected proteins, test participant IDs, predicted probabilities, input-file hash and sessionInfo().

The clean data retain global preprocessing, and the class benchmark retains full-data feature selection; this comparison is aligned with the team but is not fully leakage-free. The test set was seen earlier, making final scores exploratory. With only 31 test children, one classification changes accuracy by approximately 3.2 percentage points. Observed comparability is not proof of equivalence.
